params.text:
Purpose

The purpose of this interactive tutorial is to guide you through calculating and plotting correlations in jamovi. 

About the Study

The data that you have been using in the tutorials came from a real study conducted in December 2021. The participants were told about the study on Amazon’s Mechanical Turk (MTurk) webpage. If they decided to participate, they were immediately sent to a short online questionnaire, which asked them the questions for which we have data. The questionnaire took about 10 minutes. Participants received $3 in return for their participation.

Set up Jamovi

If you have not yet done so, download Jamovi and set it up to show numbers to 2 decimal places and p-values to 3 decimal places. See previous tutorials if you don't know how to do this. 

Data Set

1. Download the Climate Change Data.omv file from the Open Science Framework.

2. Open this dataset in Jamovi.

3. Save your Jamovi file with a file name that includes your full name and the assignment name.

Example: “Bob Brown PSYC 422 Correlations in jamovi.omv”

Jamovi Background

You may already be familiar with how to recode variables, export graphs, filter cases, and calculate descriptive statistics from other assignments; however, if you need a refresher, you could watch the following four videos:

1. Transforming scores to categories (3 minutes 42 seconds)

2. Exporting Tables and Plots (9 minutes 24 seconds)

3. Filtering cases (8 minutes 26 seconds)

4. Descriptive statistics (5 minutes 26 seconds)

Before starting this tutorial, watch the video on the following slides to learn about correlations and scatter plots. If you prefer written explanations, please review Section 4, Section 5, Section 6.3, Section 6.5, and Section 12.1 of Learning Statistics with Jamovi.

params.text:
Descriptive Statistics

To describe the people who completed this study, you will need to calculate descriptive statistics. The results of these analyses would be used in a paper to write the part of your Method section that describes your Participants.

1. Calculate the mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum age of the participants.

Note: There were 500 participants in the study and no missing data. Thus, when you are looking at the results for age, your N should be 500. If your N is not 500, you are probably using the wrong dataset, or you have forgotten to turn off a filter somewhere.

2. Use the Descriptives table for age to answer Question 1.

3. Create a new analysis. Use the frequency tables to calculate the number of people who identify as male, females and non-binary.

4. Use the Frequency table for gender to answer Question 2.

params.text:
Calculating a Correlation: Examine the Relationship Between Age and Climate Anxiety

1. Calculate a Pearson correlation for the variables Age and Climate Change Anxiety (PRCC Anxiety Subscale). To do this,

    a. Click the Regression tab and then choose Correlation Matrix.

    b. Double-click the continuous variable Age to move it to the right

    c. Double-click on the PRCC Anxiety Subscale to move it to the right

2.  Under Additional Options, check the boxes for Report significance and N, and ask for a 95% Confidence interval.

3.  Under Plot, check the boxes for Correlation Matrix, Densities for variables, and Statistics.

4. Use your results to answer the questions on the next slide.

Report the results

In Psychology, we would summarize all these results in a single sentence. This sentence uses the following format:

params.text:
A note on filtering

  • When you're creating a filter using a variable (such as PRCC Anxiety Subscale), if the variable name has spaces in it, it needs to be surrounded by quotation marks. 
  • However, these aren't the usual quotation marks! They are the mark ` which is at the top left of your keyboard (at least, it is on mine)
  • To avoid annoying error messages, it is often easier to use the little fx button in the filtering dialog box to bring the variable name into the filter
  • You can use this either for variables or for mathematical functions - in this case we're using it for variables.

params.alt: The filtering dialog box contains a little button marked fx

params.text:
Correlation between climate anxiety and climate action

  1. Filter participants to remove the people who score 50 or higher on climate anxiety (PRCC Anxiety Subscale)
  2. Calculate a Pearson correlation for between the PRCC Anxiety Subscale and CCAI Action Total.
  3. Under Additional Options, check the boxes for Report significance and N, and ask for a 95% Confidence interval.
  4. Under Plot, check the boxes for Correlation Matrix, Densities for variables, and Statistics.
  5. Make a scatter plot of the two variables in your Descriptives menu, with linear fit and standard error bar.
Fill in the missing words and numbers to report the results (numbers to 2dp, p-values to 3dp).

params.text:
Correlation between energy and water conservation

  1. Filter participants so that you are only looking at 97 participants who were less than 30 years old (using the filter age < 30). Don't forget to remove the previous filter.

  2. Calculate a Pearson correlation for your two variables.

  3. Under Additional Options, check the boxes for Report significance and N, and ask for a 95% Confidence interval.
  4. Under Plot, check the boxes for Correlation Matrix, Densities for variables, and Statistics.
  5. Make a scatter plot of the two variables in your Descriptives menu, with linear fit and standard error bar.

params.text:
Correlation between functional and cognitive-emotional impairment

  1. Keep the filter for age (participants under 30) - you should have 97 participants

  2. Calculate a Pearson correlation for PRCC - Functional Impairment and PRCC - cognitive-emotional impairment. 

  3. Under Additional Options, check the boxes for Report significance and N, and ask for a 95% Confidence interval.
  4. Under Plot, check the boxes for Correlation Matrix, Densities for variables, and Statistics.
